title: Calm By Default
eyebrow: Research and proposal · for ADHD, autistic and other neurodivergent users · nothing built yet

short.lead: I read the main guidance and research on designing for ADHD and autistic people, and checked Focus Deck against it. Seven findings came out of it, including the space audit you asked for. The biggest is to show less at once and reveal detail when asked. The full write-up with every source is in docs/plans/calm-by-default.md. This page shows what it would change, starting with the Board you found too busy.
short.hint: Tap a step for the finding, its sources and what it changes.
items: W3C's cognitive-accessibility guidance says 'Avoid too much content'. Nielsen Norman Group says to show the core first and the rest on request, two levels at most. Monotropism (Murray, Lesser and Lawson, 2005) describes attention going deeply to a few things at a time. So the Board shows one column, one quiet toolbar, and seven cards with 'Show more'.

items.alt: The calm Board: one column, a single toolbar, seven cards and Show 51 more
items.caption: The Board, calm by default.

items: Filters and the project choice sit behind 'Filter' and 'Project: All'. A card shows its title and one line; everything else is in the task panel.

items.alt: The Filter drawer open above the cards
items.caption: Filters appear only when you open them.

items: The UK Home Office autism poster says 'write in plain language' and not 'use figures of speech and idioms'. Focus Deck uses several: 'Bin it', 'slip it back in the deck', 'Stick on flags', 'Tie to tasks', 'In-tray'. The paper look can stay while the words become literal.
Calm colour and motion you control

The Home Office poster says 'use simple colours'. WCAG 2.2 and W3C say people should be able to stop motion. Focus Deck gives every project and all 45 labels a colour, and follows only the computer's 'reduce motion' setting.

Adults with ADHD in a 2026 study said starting is the hardest part, extra steps raise anxiety, and punitive overdue lists add shame (Chen, Meng and Nie, CSCW 2026). Focus Deck shows overdue tasks in red.

Nielsen Norman Group: things placed close together read as one group, so a control belongs next to what it changes. On a wide screen, Android's and Salesforce's guidance shows a list and the selected item side by side. Today the Board leaves two thirds of a 1920px-wide screen as empty columns that say 'Nothing…', and my first calm draft left 900px empty with its buttons about 650px from the list. The reworked Board keeps the list narrow enough to read comfortably and shows the selected task beside it.

items.alt: The Board at 1920 wide: a list on the left, the selected task's details beside it, the toolbar above the list
items.caption: No empty side, and every control sits next to what it changes.

items: The side menu, name and jotter as one frame

Today the side menu is 84px wide with small icons, 20px from the content, the name sits above it, outside the header, and the jotter is centred on the window, not lined up with the content. In layout A, one left column holds the name, the screens as full-size rows (icon and word side by side), and Settings at the bottom; the content starts 48px to its right, and the jotter sits at the top of the content column and is the same width as the list. On a phone, nothing changes.

items.alt: Layout A at 1920 wide: a left column with the name and four screen rows, the jotter above the list, the selected task beside the list
items.caption: Layout A: every part lines up with another part.

changes: new
Comfort settings
A Settings group for calm colours, motion and how many cards show at once.

Reduce motion (on, off, or follow the computer), calm colours (one colour per card, softer shades), and cards per chunk (5, 7 or 10). Source: W3C COGA objective 8, 'Support Adaptation and Personalization'; WCAG 2.2 criteria 2.2.2 and 2.3.3.
Only the computer's reduce-motion setting.
Three settings that change the whole app.
You set how much the app shows and moves.
choices: board
Should the Board be calm by default?
A
Yes: one column, one toolbar, cards in chunks
As in the pictures. The other columns open with one tap.
B
Calm on a phone, all three columns on a computer
A wide screen still shows everything at once.
Every source on attention agrees: fewer things on screen at once.
words
Should the app's words become literal?
A
Yes, plain words, same paper look
'Bin it' becomes 'Delete', 'Stick on flags' becomes 'Add labels', 'Tie to tasks' becomes 'Link to other tasks', 'Not this one: slip it back in the deck' becomes 'Not this one: pick another'.
B
Keep the playful words
The paper metaphor carries through the wording.
The Home Office autism poster says to avoid figures of speech, and to make buttons say exactly what they do.
colour
How should colour work?
A
One colour per card, softer shades
A card's edge shows its project category; labels are plain text until you open the task.
B
Keep project and label colours as they are
Every project and label keeps its own bright colour.
The Home Office poster asks for simple colours, not bright contrasting ones.
comfort
Add Comfort settings (motion, colour, cards per chunk)?
A
Yes, in Settings
You can adjust the app on a difficult day without changing anything else.
B
No, follow the computer's settings only
Fewer settings to look at.
W3C lists personalization as its own objective for cognitive accessibility.
overdue
How should an overdue task look?
A
Amber, with 'past its date'
Clear, but not bright red.
B
Red, as now
The strongest warning colour.
A 2026 study of adults with ADHD found punitive overdue displays add shame.
space
On a wide screen, should the selected task show beside the list?
A
Yes, list and task side by side
The space beside the list always shows something useful; on a phone the task opens full screen.
B
No, centre the list and open tasks as a panel on top
Less on screen at once, but the sides stay empty.
It uses the space for the thing you are looking at, and keeps every control next to what it changes.
frame
How should the side menu, name and jotter be laid out?
A
One left column, full-size rows, jotter in line with the list
The name, screens and Settings sit together; every screen row says its name next to its icon.
B
Today's narrow menu, made larger and set further from the content
Takes less width; labels stay under the icons.
In layout A every part of the frame lines up with another part, and the screen names are as large as the rest of the text.

wrapup.summary: Research on designing for ADHD and autistic users, with sources, and five changes that would make Focus Deck calmer.
wrapup.changing: Changed: the Board (one column, one toolbar, short cards in small groups), the side menu and header, the app's wording, colour use and overdue colour. New: Comfort settings, and the list beside the selected task on wide screens. Kept: Sort's three parts, the step bar, the focus note and the side menu of screens.
